useCases.scenario: A response needs a non-default HTTP status while retaining JSONP formatting.

interview.question: What does res.jsonp do?
interview.answer: res.jsonp(body) sends a JSON response while opting into JSONP callback support. The response is wrapped using the requested callback, such as callback({...}).
interview.followUp: How should a non-success status be sent? Call res.status(code).jsonp(body), rather than using a deprecated positional status overload.

interview.question: What can the body argument contain?
interview.answer: The body argument can be any JSON type, including null, objects, arrays, strings, numbers, or booleans. Express serializes that value and emits it with JSONP support.
interview.followUp: What should replace res.jsonp(body, status)? Use res.status(status).jsonp(body).

interview.question: How is the callback name selected?
interview.answer: The default JSONP callback name is callback. The application can override it with the jsonp callback name setting.
interview.followUp: What related response setting can improve security when responses may be interpreted as HTML? json escape makes res.json and res.jsonp escape <, >, and & as Unicode sequences.

keyPoints: Use res.jsonp when a client needs a JSON payload wrapped in a JavaScript callback invocation.
The body is the payload Express serializes and wraps; it may be omitted or undefined.
The payload is not limited to objects: primitive JSON values and null are valid too.
Serialization follows the same general response behavior as res.json, with callback wrapping added.
JSONP behavior is specifically enabled by choosing this response method instead of ordinary JSON output.
Configure the application-level jsonp callback name setting when the default callback parameter name should differ.

The older status-first overload is also deprecated; chain res.status() before res.jsonp().
Clients normally provide the callback through the callback query parameter; change the application setting if another default name is required.

res.links.explanation: Call res.links with an object whose property names are link relations and whose values are their URLs. Express converts those entries into a Link response header, then returns the response object so response methods can be chained or followed by sending the body.

parameters.name: links

example.explanation: Adds navigation URLs to the response's Link header before sending JSON.

useCases.title: Related-resource discovery
useCases.scenario: An API can expose URLs for related resources without embedding every related object in the response body.

useCases.title: HTTP hypermedia metadata
useCases.scenario: A response can describe alternate or neighboring representations using named link relations.

interview.question: What does res.links do?
interview.answer: res.links(links) accepts a Record<String, String> and returns the Response object. It joins each supplied relation-to-URL property into the HTTP Link response header.
interview.followUp: What header does a pagination example produce? It contains angle-bracketed URLs followed by rel attributes, such as `<URL>; rel="next"`.

interview.question: How do you use res.links for pagination?
interview.answer: Pass an object such as { next: '...page=2', last: '...page=5' }. Express serializes those properties into one Link header, which describes related resources or navigation targets.
interview.followUp: How would you use it in a route? Call res.links before res.json or another response-ending method so the header is set before the response is sent.

interview.question: What are the argument and return types?
interview.answer: The documented 4.x method accepts a single links argument typed as Record<String, String>. The method returns Response, allowing continued use of the response object.
interview.followUp: What changed in newer documentation? Later API documentation also permits each relation value to be an array of URL strings, but that is not the 4.x signature used here.

keyPoints: The method combines all entries into the response's Link header.
The target header is the HTTP Link header.
In Express 4.x, the argument is an object mapping relation names to URL strings.
A typical use case is exposing next and last pagination URLs from an endpoint.
gotchas: The object keys become relation names in the Link header, so use meaningful relation identifiers such as next and last.

res.locals.summary: res.locals stores values that templates rendered with res.render can use. Its values exist only for the current request-response cycle, making it suitable for request-specific data.
res.locals.explanation: res.locals is a response-scoped object for values that templates can read when res.render creates a view. Middleware can populate it during a request, and its contents disappear after that request-response cycle; use app.locals for values shared across requests.
res.locals.returns: Object used for response-local template variables.

example.title: Expose request data to a view
example.explanation: Middleware adds request-specific data to res.locals, making requestPath available when the route renders the index view.

useCases.title: View authentication context
useCases.scenario: Add authenticated-user details and authorization flags in middleware before rendering a page.

useCases.title: Request-aware rendering
useCases.scenario: Expose the current path or other request metadata to a template.

useCases.title: Per-request view configuration
useCases.scenario: Pass computed, per-request settings from middleware to a view.

interview.question: What is res.locals used for?
interview.answer: res.locals is an object attached to the response. Values placed on it become available to templates rendered with res.render during the current request.
interview.followUp: How would you expose authenticated-user information to every view? Add it in application middleware before the routes that render those views, such as res.locals.user = req.user.

interview.question: How does res.locals differ from app.locals?
interview.answer: Its values are limited to one request-response cycle and are not shared with another request. This makes it appropriate for request-level data such as a path, user, or settings.
interview.followUp: Where would you put a site-wide application name? Use app.locals rather than res.locals because the documentation directs persistent template locals to app.locals.

interview.question: How is res.locals commonly populated?
interview.answer: A middleware function can assign properties to res.locals and call next(), after which a later route can call res.render and the view can consume those properties. The documented pattern assigns user and authentication values before rendering.
interview.followUp: What security review is needed for dynamically chosen local names? Reject or constrain user-controlled keys, because view-engine handling of sensitive keys can create security issues.

keyPoints: Assign template inputs to res.locals before calling res.render so the view can access them.
Its scope follows the current response lifecycle rather than the whole application.
Typical values include request metadata, authenticated-user data, and per-request settings.
The view engine reads these properties while producing the rendered response.
Treat local-property names as security-sensitive, especially when they could influence view-engine behavior.
gotchas: Do not use untrusted input as local-variable keys: view engines may interpret those keys in unsafe ways, including creating a cross-site scripting path.
res.locals does not persist between requests; choose app.locals when the value should remain available across request cycles.

res.location.summary: res.location(path) sets the HTTP Location response header to a specified URL or path. It returns the response object and does not validate the resulting URL.
res.location.explanation: Call res.location(path) to set the HTTP Location response header. Express encodes the supplied value when needed and returns the response object, so it can be chained with other response methods; it does not validate the resulting URL.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: The URL to set in the Location header.

example.title: Set a response Location header
example.explanation: Run the server, then request /old and inspect the Location response header.

useCases.title: Set Location without redirecting
useCases.scenario: Expose the destination of a response while controlling the status and body separately.

useCases.title: Advertise an internal path
useCases.scenario: Provide a relative application route as the response destination.

useCases.title: Advertise an external URL
useCases.scenario: Provide an absolute destination URL in an HTTP response.

interview.question: What does res.location() do?
interview.answer: res.location(path) sets the response's Location header to the supplied path and returns the Response object. It does not itself perform a redirect; a separate response action, such as a status and send, is needed.
interview.followUp: What security concern should be considered? The method passes the encoded URL onward without validation, so untrusted redirect targets must be constrained or validated.

interview.question: What argument does res.location() accept?
interview.answer: The path argument is a string identifying the URL to place in the Location header. It can be a path such as /foo/bar or an absolute URL such as http://example.com.
interview.followUp: What happens if the path is not already encoded? Express encodes it before placing it in the header.

interview.question: How did the back value behave, and what replaced it?
interview.answer: The special back value refers to the request's Referer header, or / when that header is absent. In Express 4.21.0 it was deprecated, so newer code should use req.get('Referrer') || /.
interview.followUp: Why is the fallback useful? It ensures the replacement argument remains defined when the client did not send a referrer.

keyPoints: The method writes the supplied path into the response's Location header.
Its path argument represents the URL value that the response should advertise.
The API accepts relative paths, absolute URLs, and the documented back form.
After receiving the header, the browser determines how the location relates to the current page and referring URL.
gotchas: Express does not validate the URL before sending it; validate or constrain input when the value is user-controlled.
Do not use the special back value in new code; use the request Referrer header with / as the fallback.
The back value depends on the incoming Referer header and therefore may resolve differently for different requests.

res.send.summary: Sends an HTTP response from an Express route or middleware. Express formats strings as HTML, objects and arrays as JSON, and buffers as binary data.
res.send.explanation: Call `res.send(body)` inside a route handler to complete the HTTP response. Express selects the response representation from the value: strings are treated as HTML, objects and arrays as JSON, and buffers as binary data; the method returns the response object for chaining.

parameters.name: body
parameters.type: String | Buffer | Object | Array | Boolean | undefined
parameters.description: The response content. Strings are sent as HTML, objects and arrays as JSON, and buffers as binary data; the documented type also includes Boolean and undefined.

example.title: Send a string response
example.explanation: Creates a route that sends a string response for a requested user ID.

useCases.title: Send HTML text
useCases.scenario: A route returns a rendered or markup-like response directly to the client.

useCases.title: Return JSON data
useCases.scenario: An endpoint returns structured application data without manually serializing it.

useCases.title: Send a buffer
useCases.scenario: A handler needs to transmit already-created binary content.

interview.question: What does `res.send()` do, and what body types does it accept?
interview.answer: `res.send(body)` sends the HTTP response and returns the `Response` object. Express treats strings as HTML, objects and arrays as JSON, and buffers as binary data.
interview.followUp: How would you return a JSON error with a non-200 status? Chain the status setter: `res.status(500).send({ error: 'something blew up' })`.

interview.question: How does Express handle different response-body types?
interview.answer: The documented body argument may be a string, buffer, object, array, boolean, or undefined. The method chooses handling based on the supplied value, including HTML for strings and JSON for objects or arrays.
interview.followUp: What should be done with a numeric body? Convert it to a string first, such as `res.send(String(123))`, so it is not treated as a status code.

interview.question: How should a response status be set when using `res.send()`?
interview.answer: Set the status separately by chaining `res.status(status).send(body)`. The older positional forms are deprecated, including `res.send(body, status)` and `res.send(status)` in Express 4.5.0, with the reversed form deprecated in 4.7.0.
interview.followUp: Which method sends only a status code? Use `res.sendStatus(status)`.

keyPoints: The required conceptual input is the response body supplied to the method.
Express maps strings to HTML, objects and arrays to JSON, and buffers to binary responses.
Calling the method completes the response sent to the client.
Supported body values include buffers, strings, objects, booleans, and arrays.
A status can be assigned before sending by chaining `res.status(code).send(body)`.
gotchas: Do not pass the status as a positional argument; use `res.status(status).send(body)` instead.
Use `res.sendStatus()` when the response should contain only a status code.
A numeric argument can be interpreted as a status code, so convert numeric body data with `String(value)`.

res.sendFile.summary: res.sendFile() transfers a file from the server filesystem to the client. It accepts a path, optional serving options, and an optional callback for completion or errors.
res.sendFile.explanation: Use res.sendFile() to transfer one file to the client. Supply an absolute path, or provide root so the path can be relative; options configure file-serving behavior, and an optional callback handles completion or errors.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Path to the file to transfer; it must be absolute unless options.root is set.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional file-serving settings, including maxAge, root, lastModified, and headers.

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: Optional callback invoked after completion or on error; receives err.

res.sendFile.returns: The documentation describes the transfer and callback behavior but does not specify a separate return value.

example.title: Serve a file from a constrained directory
example.explanation: Serves the requested file relative to a fixed directory and forwards transfer errors to Express.

useCases.title: Serve a specific file
useCases.scenario: A route needs to return one known HTML, image, PDF, or other filesystem file.

useCases.title: Serve files under a fixed root
useCases.scenario: A request selects a filename within a controlled directory.

useCases.title: Customize file response metadata
useCases.scenario: A response needs custom caching or HTTP headers for one file.

interview.question: What does res.sendFile() do, and what path form does it require?
interview.answer: It transfers the file at the supplied path and sets Content-Type from the filename extension. The path must be absolute unless options.root is supplied.
interview.followUp: How would you safely serve a user-selected file? Use a fixed absolute root and pass a relative name, then handle callback errors with next(err).

interview.question: Which important options does the documentation describe?
interview.answer: The options object configures serving, including maxAge, root, lastModified, and headers. maxAge defaults to 0, while lastModified defaults to true.
interview.followUp: What cache-related behavior can be changed? Set maxAge for Cache-Control max-age and set lastModified to false to suppress Last-Modified.

interview.question: How does the callback affect error handling?
interview.answer: The optional fn(err) callback runs after transfer completion or when an error occurs. If an error occurs while using it, the callback must finish the response or delegate to the next route.
interview.followUp: What should a typical Express handler do on failure? Call next(err), unless it deliberately sends or ends an error response.

keyPoints: The method sends one filesystem file as the response.
Express derives the response media type from the file extension.
The optional options object customizes file delivery.
By default, the file's operating-system modification time is exposed through Last-Modified.
Use options.headers to add or override headers for the file response.
The callback receives an error value when transfer fails and is also called after completion.
gotchas: Without root, path must be absolute.
Treat user-derived absolute paths as a security boundary and construct them securely.
When using the callback, end the response or pass the error to the next route.
Relative paths may contain .. with root, so choose a trusted root and understand the resulting resolution.

res.sendStatus.summary: res.sendStatus(statusCode) sets an HTTP status and sends its registered status message as a text response. For an unknown code, the body is the numeric code itself.
res.sendStatus.explanation: Call this response method with an HTTP status number to set the response status and immediately send its registered status message as plain text. If the number is not recognized, Express sends the numeric code as the body instead; the method returns the response object for chaining or inspection.

parameters.name: statusCode
parameters.description: HTTP status code to set; its registered status message becomes the response body.

example.title: Send a 404 status response
example.explanation: Run the server and request /missing to receive a 404 response whose text body is the registered status message.

useCases.title: Return a not-found response
useCases.scenario: A route cannot find the requested resource and needs to return the conventional 404 status text.

useCases.title: Send a simple status-only response
useCases.scenario: A health, readiness, or validation endpoint needs only a status and standard text message.

useCases.title: Reject a request concisely
useCases.scenario: A route must reject a request without constructing a custom body.

interview.question: What does res.sendStatus(statusCode) do?
interview.answer: It accepts one numeric status code, sets that code on the response, and sends the corresponding registered status message as text. It returns the Response object.
interview.followUp: What happens for an unrecognized code? Express sends the code number as the response body rather than a registered message.

interview.question: When would you choose res.status().send() instead?
interview.answer: Use res.sendStatus() when the response consists of a status and its standard text message. Use res.status().send() when the body must be custom or contain structured data.
interview.followUp: How would you return a JSON error? Set the status separately, then call res.json() with the error object.

interview.question: What are the argument and return value?
interview.answer: The argument is a Number representing the HTTP status code to set. The method returns Response, so the returned object is the Express response.
interview.followUp: What should callers do if they need a different content type or message? Use res.status(statusCode) followed by an appropriate sending method.

keyPoints: The numeric argument selects both the HTTP status and, for recognized codes, the default text body.
It completes the response by sending the status message as text rather than leaving the response open.
Unknown codes are supported with a numeric body instead of a named status phrase.
gotchas: Unrecognized status codes do not produce a named status message; the numeric code itself becomes the response body.

res.set.summary: Sets one or more HTTP response headers. Use a field/value pair for one header or an object for several headers, and chain the returned response object.
res.set.explanation: Use res.set() in a route handler to assign HTTP response headers. Pass a field and value for one header, or pass an object containing several header-value pairs; the method returns the response object so calls can be chained.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: The response header field name, or an object mapping header names to values.

parameters.name: val
parameters.description: The value for the selected response header field.

example.title: Set response headers
example.explanation: Sets individual and multiple response headers before sending a plain-text response.

useCases.title: Content type and length
useCases.scenario: Set content metadata before returning a body.

useCases.title: Cache-control policy
useCases.scenario: Apply browser or intermediary caching directives.

useCases.title: Custom response headers
useCases.scenario: Add application-specific metadata to an outgoing response.

interview.question: What does res.set() do, and what forms of input does it accept?
interview.answer: res.set() assigns headers on the outgoing HTTP response. It accepts either one header name with its value or an object containing multiple headers.
interview.followUp: What happens if it follows res.append()? The set operation resets the previously appended header value.

interview.question: What is the signature of res.set()?
interview.answer: The single-header form is res.set(field, [val]), while the object form is res.set(field). The object form is useful when several headers must be configured together.
interview.followUp: How can you set both cache policy and a custom header? Pass an object with both field-value pairs to res.set().

interview.question: When should res.set() be called in a route?
interview.answer: Headers should be configured before the response is completed, such as before calling res.send(). The method belongs to Express's response object and is used inside a request handler.
interview.followUp: What should be checked when a header appears missing? Verify that the header was set before the response was sent and that a later operation did not replace it.

keyPoints: The method assigns a named HTTP response header to the supplied value.
A header can be set with a field name followed by a string value.
An object lets one call configure multiple response headers.
gotchas: Calling res.set() after res.append() replaces the value previously added by res.append().

res.status.summary: res.status(code) sets an Express response’s HTTP status code and returns the response object for chaining. Use it before methods that send or finish the response.
res.status.explanation: Call res.status(code) to assign the HTTP status for the response. Because it returns the Response object, chain it with methods such as json(), send(), end(), or sendFile() to complete the response.

parameters.name: code
parameters.description: The numeric HTTP status code to set on the response.

example.title: Set a response status before sending JSON
example.explanation: Run this Express app and request /health to receive a JSON response with HTTP status 200.

useCases.title: Send a status with text or JSON
useCases.scenario: An endpoint must report a client or server outcome while returning a body.

useCases.title: Set a status and end the response
useCases.scenario: A handler must finish without returning content.

useCases.title: Set a status before sending a file
useCases.scenario: A route returns a file but needs a non-default status.

interview.question: What does res.status() do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: res.status(code) sets the HTTP status code and returns the Response object. Its chainable return makes patterns such as res.status(400).send('Bad Request') possible.
interview.followUp: How would you send only a status and its standard text? Use res.sendStatus(code), which sets the status and sends the registered status message.

interview.question: What argument does res.status() accept?
interview.answer: The argument is code, a Number representing the HTTP status code for the response. The method is a chainable alias of Node’s response.statusCode.
interview.followUp: What should follow res.status() when the request must be completed? Chain a method such as end(), send(), json(), or sendFile().

interview.question: How should status and a JSON body be sent together?
interview.answer: Use res.status() separately before sending a body, for example res.status(500).json({ error: 'message' }). This is the documented replacement for deprecated status arguments on older response-method signatures.
interview.followUp: Why avoid res.json(body, status) in modern Express code? Its positional status form is deprecated; set the status separately and chain the response method.

keyPoints: The method assigns the HTTP status code that Express will use for the outgoing response.
The returned Response object enables fluent response construction.
Call end() after setting a status when no response body is needed.
Combine a status with send() to return a body in the same operation.
The status can also precede sendFile() when returning a file response.
gotchas: Pass a numeric HTTP status code; this method is not the replacement for sending a status-only response body.
The method changes the response status code but does not itself send or finish the response; chain a terminating response method.

res.statusCode.summary: `res.statusCode` sets the HTTP status code on an Express response. Assign it before sending or ending the response, or use chainable `res.status(code)`.
res.statusCode.explanation: `res.statusCode` is the Node.js response property exposed by Express. Assign a valid HTTP status code before sending the response; Express also provides `res.status(code)` as a chainable alternative.

parameters.name: statusCode
parameters.description: The numeric HTTP status code to assign to the response.

res.statusCode.returns: No separate return value; this is a response property assignment. The related `res.status(code)` method returns the Response object.

example.title: Set a response status directly
example.explanation: This route assigns the response status directly, then sends a JSON body.

useCases.title: Set a custom status with JSON or text
useCases.scenario: A handler must return a precise protocol status together with a response body.

useCases.title: Prepare status in middleware
useCases.scenario: Middleware determines the outcome before a later handler sends the response.

useCases.title: Use the chainable Express equivalent
useCases.scenario: Application code prefers fluent response construction.

interview.question: What does `res.statusCode` control?
interview.answer: `res.statusCode` is the response property used to select the HTTP status code. Set it before a response-ending operation such as `res.json()` or `res.end()`.
interview.followUp: How can the same status be set in Express style? Use `res.status(code)`, which is chainable.

interview.question: What values are safe to assign?
interview.answer: The documented valid range is 100 through 599. Values outside that range may cause some Node.js versions to throw.
interview.followUp: What should an application do when status input is user-controlled? Validate or map it to an allowed status before assignment.

interview.question: How does `res.status()` relate to `res.statusCode`?
interview.answer: `res.status(code)` sets the HTTP status and returns the response, allowing calls such as `res.status(400).send(...)`. It is documented as a chainable alias of Node’s `response.statusCode`.
interview.followUp: When only a status and its standard text are needed, use `res.sendStatus(code)` instead.

keyPoints: The property belongs to the response object available in route handlers and middleware.
Express exposes this Node response property because its response object extends Node’s native response.
Assigning a number selects the status code that will accompany the response.
For Express-style code, `res.status(code)` provides a chainable way to perform the same status selection.
gotchas: Use a valid HTTP status code; some Node.js versions throw for values outside the permitted range.

res.statusMessage.summary: `res.statusMessage` is the HTTP reason phrase associated with an Express response’s status code. Express’s error handler derives it from the final status code, while application code may assign a custom phrase.
res.statusMessage.explanation: `res.statusMessage` is the response property used for the HTTP reason phrase associated with the status code. Express’s error handling sets it according to the response status code; applications can also assign a custom value before ending the response.

example.title: Set a response status message
example.explanation: Sets a custom reason phrase alongside the response status code.

useCases.title: Provide a custom HTTP reason phrase
useCases.scenario: Custom protocol responses

useCases.title: Reflect the normalized error status
useCases.scenario: Error middleware

useCases.title: Set response metadata before ending
useCases.scenario: Low-level response handling

interview.question: What is `res.statusMessage` used for in Express?
interview.answer: It is the HTTP reason phrase sent with the response status line, such as `Not Found` for status 404. Express uses it during error handling based on the status code.
interview.followUp: What happens if an error provides an invalid status? Express normalizes status values outside the 4xx or 5xx ranges to 500, then derives the message from that status.

interview.question: Does `res.statusMessage` determine the response body?
interview.answer: Express sets `res.statusMessage` according to the status code when an error response is written. It is separate from the response body, which Express generates according to the environment.
interview.followUp: How can an application control the body independently? Set the status and message properties, then explicitly send or end the response with the desired body.

interview.question: How does error handling relate `res.statusMessage` to the response body?
interview.answer: No. The error handler sets the status message from the status code, while the body is the status-code HTML in production or the error stack otherwise. The two response components are handled separately.
interview.followUp: What other error information can be added? Headers supplied through an `err.headers` object are also added to the response.

keyPoints: During Express error handling, the reason phrase is selected from the resulting HTTP status code.
An error’s `status` or `statusCode` influences the status code that Express uses before determining the status message.
Invalid error status values are replaced with 500, so the corresponding message is based on the normalized status.
gotchas: When Express writes an error response, it derives the status message from the status code; assigning a custom value may replace that phrase.

res.type.summary: Sets the response Content-Type from a MIME type or file extension. Values containing `/` are used literally; other values undergo extension-based MIME lookup.
res.type.explanation: `res.type(type)` sets the response’s `Content-Type`. A value containing `/` is used directly; otherwise Express treats it as a file extension and looks up the corresponding MIME type.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: A MIME type or a file extension used to determine the response Content-Type.

example.title: Set a JSON response type
example.explanation: Sets the response MIME type to JSON before sending the payload.

useCases.title: Declare JSON responses
useCases.scenario: An endpoint returns JSON and needs an explicit JSON media type.

useCases.title: Resolve a standard extension
useCases.scenario: A route serves content whose format is identified by a known extension.

useCases.title: Set a custom MIME type
useCases.scenario: An API must emit a vendor-specific or other custom media type.

interview.question: What does res.type() do?
interview.answer: It accepts a MIME type or an extension and returns the response object. Extensions are resolved through Express’s MIME mapping, while values containing `/` are applied literally.
interview.followUp: What does `res.type('json')` do? It looks up the JSON MIME type and sets the Content-Type accordingly.

interview.question: How are extensions handled?
interview.answer: `res.type('.html')` and `res.type('html')` both select the HTML MIME type. The leading dot is optional for extension lookup.
interview.followUp: How would you set a custom media type? Pass the complete value, such as `application/vnd.example+json`, because it contains `/`.

interview.question: What does res.type() return?
interview.answer: The method changes the response Content-Type header and returns `res`, allowing response methods to be chained. It does not itself send the response.
interview.followUp: Why might setting the type before `send()` matter? The later body-sending operation can use the selected type when constructing the HTTP response.

keyPoints: The method sets the response’s Content-Type header based on the supplied value.
The argument can be either a complete MIME type or a file extension.
Values without `/` are interpreted as extensions rather than literal media types.
In Express 4.x, extension resolution uses the mapping exposed through express.static.mime.lookup().
An HTML extension resolves to the text/html media type.
The json extension resolves to application/json.

Router.summary: `express.Router()` creates a modular, mountable router that combines middleware and route handlers. Add routes to it and mount it with `app.use()` or another router.
Router.explanation: `express.Router()` creates a self-contained routing and middleware object. Define middleware and HTTP-method handlers on it, then mount it with `app.use()` so its paths are resolved relative to the mount point.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options object controlling router behavior, including `caseSensitive`, `mergeParams`, and `strict`.

example.title: Mount a modular router
example.explanation: Creates a mountable router, adds router-level middleware and a GET route, then mounts it beneath a parameterized application path.

useCases.title: Modular route organization
useCases.scenario: Group endpoints for a feature or resource in a dedicated module.

useCases.title: Scoped middleware
useCases.scenario: Attach authentication, logging, or other middleware only to one route group.

useCases.title: Mountable route modules
useCases.scenario: Reuse the same route bundle beneath different application mount paths.

interview.question: What is an Express Router, and why use one?
interview.answer: `express.Router()` returns a router object that combines middleware and routing behavior. It can be passed to `app.use()` or mounted on another router, making it suitable for modular route groups.
interview.followUp: How does mounting affect a route path? A route such as `/events` on a router mounted at `/calendar` is reached through the combined path `/calendar/events`.

interview.question: What does the `mergeParams` option do?
interview.answer: `mergeParams` preserves parameter values from the parent router; its default is `false`. If parent and child routers use the same parameter name, the child value wins.
interview.followUp: When should it be enabled? Enable it when handlers in the child need parameters captured by the parent mount path.

interview.question: How are routes and middleware added to a router?
interview.answer: `router.METHOD()` methods, such as `router.get()` and `router.post()`, define handlers for particular HTTP methods. `router.route(path)` returns a single route object that can then receive multiple HTTP-verb handlers.
interview.followUp: How can middleware be applied across methods? Use `router.use()` for router-level middleware, or pass middleware callbacks to a method-specific route.

keyPoints: A router combines middleware and route handling in one reusable object.
It is a focused mini-application rather than a complete standalone Express application.
Mount it with `app.use()` to integrate its middleware and routes into the application pipeline.
Call `express.Router()` to construct a new router.
After construction, add router-level middleware and HTTP-method handlers using application-like APIs.
Use lowercase HTTP-method methods such as `get`, `post`, and `put` for method-specific routing.
gotchas: Use `next('router')` when a condition should leave the current router and return control to the outer middleware chain.
Multiple callbacks can be supplied, but a callback that calls `next('route')` skips the remaining callbacks for that route.

RouterOptions.summary: RouterOptions is the optional configuration object for express.Router(). It controls case sensitivity, parent-parameter inheritance, and strict trailing-slash matching; each option defaults to false.
RouterOptions.explanation: RouterOptions is the optional object accepted by express.Router([options]). Its three documented settings control URL case matching, inheritance of parent route parameters, and treatment of trailing slashes; omitted settings default to false.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional configuration object for router behavior; omitted properties default to false.

parameters.name: options.caseSensitive
parameters.description: Enables case-sensitive matching; default false.

parameters.name: options.mergeParams
parameters.description: Preserves parent-router req.params; default false.

parameters.name: options.strict
parameters.description: Enables strict routing for trailing slashes; default false.

RouterOptions.returns: Router — a router object to which middleware and HTTP method routes can be added.

example.title: Configuring an Express router
example.explanation: Creates a router that distinguishes URL case and trailing slashes while retaining parameters inherited from its mounted parent route.

useCases.title: Nested resource routes
useCases.scenario: A mounted child router must read an identifier captured by its parent path.

useCases.title: Case-sensitive endpoints
useCases.scenario: An API requires URLs whose capitalization carries meaning.

useCases.title: Strict URL conventions
useCases.scenario: An application must distinguish canonical paths with and without trailing slashes.

interview.question: What is RouterOptions and what does it configure?
interview.answer: RouterOptions is the optional configuration object passed to express.Router. It supports caseSensitive, mergeParams, and strict, and the router is returned for adding middleware and routes.
interview.followUp: How would a mounted router access a parameter from its parent path? Pass mergeParams: true when constructing the router; otherwise the parent parameter is not preserved.

interview.question: What does caseSensitive do?
interview.answer: caseSensitive enables case-sensitive path matching. Its default is false, so paths such as /Foo and /foo are treated as equivalent.
interview.followUp: What effect does strict have instead? It controls trailing-slash matching, making /foo and /foo/ distinct when enabled.

interview.question: What does mergeParams change?
interview.answer: mergeParams preserves req.params values from the parent router when a child router is mounted. If names conflict, the child parameter takes precedence.
interview.followUp: When is this useful? It is useful for nested routes whose handlers need an identifier captured by the mounting path.

keyPoints: RouterOptions is an optional object used to configure the behavior of a router created by express.Router.
caseSensitive makes route matching distinguish uppercase and lowercase characters.
strict makes the router treat a path with a trailing slash differently from the same path without one.
mergeParams carries route parameters from the parent router into the child router.
gotchas: With mergeParams enabled, a child parameter with the same name as a parent parameter overrides the inherited value.
strict is false by default, so paths differing only by a trailing slash normally match identically.

serveStatic.summary: serveStatic(root, options) creates middleware that serves files from a root directory based on the request URL. Missing files fall through to next(), allowing fallback middleware or multiple static directories.
serveStatic.explanation: Calling serveStatic with a root directory creates middleware that maps the request URL onto that directory and serves a matching file. If no file matches, it calls next() rather than ending the request, so multiple static directories or fallback handlers can be composed.

parameters.name: root
parameters.description: Filesystem root directory from which requested files are served.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional configuration, including index, extensions, and setHeaders behavior.

serveStatic.returns: A middleware function that serves files from the specified root and calls next() when a file is not found.

example.title: Serve a public directory
example.explanation: Serves files from the absolute public directory and lets later middleware handle requests for missing files.

useCases.title: Static asset hosting
useCases.scenario: Serve browser assets such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images from a public directory.

useCases.title: Fallback resolution
useCases.scenario: Try a second directory or route handler after the first static location has no matching file.

useCases.title: Custom response headers
useCases.scenario: Apply cache-control or other response headers while serving files.

interview.question: What does serveStatic do when a requested file is absent?
interview.answer: serveStatic(root, options) returns middleware that serves files below root. It combines the request URL with root, and calls next() when no file is found.
interview.followUp: How can static fallbacks be composed? Mount multiple serveStatic instances in sequence; a miss in one allows the next middleware to try.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the root argument?
interview.answer: The root directory is the base used to locate requested files. The middleware uses the request URL together with that root to determine which file to send.
interview.followUp: How should an application serve a directory reliably regardless of its launch directory? Resolve or construct an absolute root path before passing it to serveStatic.

interview.question: How does the index option affect directory requests?
interview.answer: The index option controls directory requests. By default index.html is sent; false disables index serving, while a string or ordered array selects alternative names.
interview.followUp: How could different default documents be tried in order? Pass an array such as ['default.html', 'default.htm'] as index.

keyPoints: The function creates middleware for serving files beneath the supplied root directory.
A request URL is combined with the root to locate the file that should be served.
A missing file falls through to the next middleware, enabling fallback handlers and stacked static roots.
The extensions option can try alternate filename extensions when the original file is absent.
When extension fallbacks are configured, the first existing candidate is returned.
The setHeaders option provides a callback for applying custom response headers.
gotchas: A missing file is passed to the next middleware rather than producing a 404 response here.
Directory requests serve index.html by default; change or disable this with the index option.
A setHeaders callback must modify response headers synchronously.

static.summary: express.static serves static assets from a root directory through Express middleware. An optional options object controls file lookup, caching, dotfiles, ETags, and response headers.
static.explanation: express.static creates built-in middleware that maps request URLs to files below a chosen root directory. Mount it directly for ordinary paths or under a route prefix for a virtual URL path; optional settings control file lookup, caching, dotfiles, headers, and related serving behavior.

parameters.name: root
parameters.description: Root directory from which static assets are served.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings controlling how files are served, including dotfiles, ETags, extensions, caching, and headers.

example.title: Serve files under a virtual URL prefix
example.explanation: Run the app from the project directory, place a file such as public/style.css there, then request /static/style.css.

useCases.title: Serve a public asset directory
useCases.scenario: Expose frontend assets such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images from a public directory.

useCases.title: Add a virtual path prefix
useCases.scenario: Make assets available below a URL prefix such as /static without changing their filesystem location.

useCases.title: Combine multiple asset directories
useCases.scenario: Search several asset directories in order, giving earlier registrations precedence.

interview.question: What does express.static do?
interview.answer: It is Express's built-in middleware for serving static assets. It combines the request URL with the configured root directory to determine which file to serve.
interview.followUp: How can the same middleware expose files below a different URL prefix? Mount it with app.use('/prefix', express.static(root)); the prefix is virtual and need not exist on disk.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the root argument?
interview.answer: The root argument identifies the directory containing the assets. The function resolves the requested file by combining req.url with that root.
interview.followUp: What is a common way to avoid dependence on the launch directory? Pass an absolute root path, commonly constructed from the application's directory.

interview.question: How do you customize static-file serving?
interview.answer: Pass an options object as the second argument. It can configure behavior such as dotfiles, ETags, extension fallbacks, immutable caching, and custom response headers.
interview.followUp: How can multiple asset directories be searched? Register express.static more than once; earlier middleware gets precedence when it serves a matching file.

keyPoints: express.static is available as Express-provided middleware rather than requiring a separately installed application middleware package.
The middleware delegates its underlying static-file behavior to the serve-static implementation.
The root directory is the source tree from which requested static assets are exposed.
File selection joins the incoming request URL with the configured root to locate the asset.
The options object can turn ETag generation on or off.
The setHeaders option can apply response headers for each served file.
gotchas: A relative root is resolved from the process's launch directory, not automatically from the source file's directory; use an absolute path when that distinction matters.
The middleware's ETag behavior is weak and cannot be treated as strong validation.
Enabling extension fallbacks can make a request resolve to the first matching extension, so configure the list deliberately.

strict routing.summary: `express.Router({ strict: true })` makes trailing slashes significant when matching routes. By default, `/foo` and `/foo/` are treated as the same path.
strict routing.explanation: Pass `strict: true` to `express.Router()` to make trailing slashes significant for routes managed by that router. With the default setting, a path such as `/events` also matches `/events/`; strict routing separates those two forms.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional router configuration object; its `strict` Boolean controls whether trailing slashes distinguish paths.

example.title: Strict router paths
example.explanation: Creates a router where `/events` and `/events/` are distinct paths, then mounts it under `/calendar`.

useCases.title: Enforce URL shape
useCases.scenario: An API needs canonical URL forms and should reject requests that add or omit a trailing slash.

useCases.title: Configure a sub-router
useCases.scenario: A mounted feature router must use stricter path matching without changing unrelated routers.

useCases.title: Distinguish trailing-slash routes
useCases.scenario: Two endpoints intentionally differ only by whether the path ends in a slash.

interview.question: How do you enable strict routing for an Express router?
interview.answer: Set the router option to `strict: true`, for example `express.Router({ strict: true })`. This makes `/foo` and `/foo/` different paths.
interview.followUp: What happens when the option is omitted? The router defaults to non-strict behavior, treating both forms as equivalent.

interview.question: What is the default value and behavior of the router's `strict` option?
interview.answer: The option is Boolean and defaults to `false`. Therefore, a router normally treats `/foo` and `/foo/` as the same route.
interview.followUp: How would you make only one router strict? Create that router with `strict: true`; other routers can retain their own options.

interview.question: How would you apply strict routing to a mounted sub-router?
interview.answer: Use `express.Router({ strict: true })`, add routes to the returned router, and mount it with `app.use()`. The router remains middleware-compatible while applying its route-matching policy.
interview.followUp: Can strict routing be combined with case sensitivity? Yes; pass both options, such as `{ caseSensitive: true, strict: true }`.

keyPoints: The option accepts a Boolean and defaults to `false`.
Setting the option to `true` enables strict route matching.
Without strict routing, a route and its trailing-slash variant are equivalent.
gotchas: Strict routing is off unless explicitly enabled, so relying on the default can unintentionally accept both trailing-slash forms.
The option controls trailing-slash matching, not general path matching or HTTP-method behavior.

trust proxy.summary: `trust proxy` configures whether and how Express trusts a front-facing proxy and its `X-Forwarded-*` headers. It affects client IP and related request properties.
trust proxy.explanation: Set this application option when Express is behind a front-facing proxy and should interpret forwarded connection details. Its value controls which proxy hops are trusted, so Express can derive client IP-related request properties and other proxy-aware values.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Boolean, string, number, function, or array defining which proxy hops or addresses to trust.

trust proxy.returns: The configured application setting; its effects are observed through proxy-aware request properties such as req.ip and req.ips.

example.title: Trust a loopback proxy
example.explanation: This runnable Express app trusts loopback as a proxy network and exposes the proxy-aware request values.

useCases.title: Recover client IP information
useCases.scenario: An Express server runs behind a reverse proxy and must identify the originating client.

useCases.title: Restrict trust to known networks
useCases.scenario: A deployment uses known proxy subnets or named private networks.

useCases.title: Trust a proxy hop count
useCases.scenario: A fixed proxy chain has a known maximum hop count.

useCases.title: Reflect forwarded protocol
useCases.scenario: HTTPS termination occurs before requests reach Express.

interview.question: What is the purpose of trust proxy?
interview.answer: It is an application setting that tells Express the app is behind a front-facing proxy and permits use of X-Forwarded-* information. It is disabled by default.
interview.followUp: What does a numeric value mean? It trusts the nth hop from the front-facing proxy as the client.

interview.question: How do the supported value types differ?
interview.answer: A boolean true treats the leftmost forwarded entry as the client, while false treats the app as directly internet-facing and uses the connection's remote address. An IP, subnet, or array limits trust to specified proxy addresses or networks.
interview.followUp: Which policy is safer than a blanket true in a known topology? Specify trusted proxy addresses, subnets, or an appropriate hop count.

interview.question: Which request properties change when proxy trust is enabled?
interview.answer: When enabled, Express derives req.ip and req.ips using the socket address and X-Forwarded-For, stopping at the first untrusted address. It also derives req.hostname from X-Forwarded-Host and reflects X-Forwarded-Proto through req.protocol.
interview.followUp: Why must forwarded headers be controlled by the proxy? Because client-controlled headers can otherwise influence these request values.

keyPoints: The setting accepts booleans, strings, numbers, functions, or arrays, and starts disabled.
It enables Express to interpret forwarded headers when the application is deployed behind a front-facing proxy.
Express resolves the apparent client address through one or more trusted proxy hops.
The resulting proxy chain is available through req.ips as an array of addresses.
String and array configurations identify the proxy addresses or networks that Express should trust.
A numeric setting defines trust by hop count from the front-facing proxy.
Express delegates the trust calculation to the proxy-addr package.
gotchas: A custom trust function is powerful but risky; use it only when the proxy topology and forwarded headers are understood.
Trusting every proxy with true can accept a client-supplied leftmost forwarded address, so use a narrower trust policy when appropriate.
After enabling proxy trust, hostname data may come from a header that the client can set unless the proxy overwrites or controls it.

use.summary: app.use() binds application-level middleware to an Express app, globally or under a path. Middleware can handle a request, modify it, end the response, or pass control onward with next().
use.explanation: app.use() attaches middleware to an Express application. It can apply middleware globally or under a path, and middleware controls whether processing ends or continues by sending a response or calling next().

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Path or route where the middleware applies.

parameters.name: middleware
parameters.description: Middleware function to invoke for matching requests.

use.returns: The documentation does not specify a return value for app.use().

example.title: Path-scoped application middleware
example.explanation: Mounts application-level middleware for requests matching the path, then passes control to the route handler.

useCases.title: Cross-cutting application middleware
useCases.scenario: Apply logging, authentication, parsing, or other shared processing across application requests.

useCases.title: Path-scoped processing
useCases.scenario: Run middleware only for a URL subtree such as /user/:id.

useCases.title: Middleware chains
useCases.scenario: Compose several middleware functions into an ordered request pipeline.

interview.question: What does app.use() do?
interview.answer: app.use() binds application-level middleware to an Express app. With a path argument, the middleware applies to requests matching that path; without one, it can run for every request.
interview.followUp: How do you attach middleware to only one HTTP method? Use app.METHOD(), such as app.get() or app.post(), with the method-specific handler.

interview.question: How does middleware continue request processing?
interview.answer: A middleware function receives req, res, and next. It can execute code, modify the request or response, end the cycle, or call next() to transfer control to the following middleware.
interview.followUp: What happens if it neither ends the cycle nor calls next()? The request remains unresolved and can hang.

interview.question: Why does middleware order matter?
interview.answer: Middleware is executed in registration order, so app.use() placement determines when it runs relative to other middleware and routes. A path-scoped middleware can inspect route parameters when mounted appropriately.
interview.followUp: How is router-level middleware expressed? Use router.use() and router.METHOD() on an Express Router instance.

keyPoints: Use app.use() to register middleware on an Express application instance.
The middleware argument contains the request-processing function.
Middleware may run code, modify req or res, finish the response, or delegate to another middleware.

views.summary: The `views` application setting identifies the directory, or ordered directories, that Express uses to find view templates. It defaults to `process.cwd() + '/views'`.
views.explanation: The `views` application setting tells Express where templates are stored. It accepts one directory or an ordered list of directories; rendering searches that list in order, and its default is a `views` directory under the current working directory.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Application setting name, which must be `views` when reading or configuring this setting.

views.returns: The configured value of the `views` application setting when read with `app.get('views')`.

example.title: Configure application view directories
example.explanation: Configures two view directories; Express searches them in array order when resolving a template.

useCases.title: Custom template location
useCases.scenario: Store templates outside the conventional project directory.

useCases.title: Multiple template directories
useCases.scenario: Combine project templates with reusable templates from another directory.

useCases.title: Ordered fallback lookup
useCases.scenario: Control which duplicate template name takes precedence.

interview.question: What does the `views` setting control?
interview.answer: `views` is an Express application setting containing either a string directory or an array of directories. Its default is `process.cwd() + '/views'`.
interview.followUp: What happens with an array? Express checks directories in their listed order and uses the first matching view.

interview.question: What types can the `views` setting have?
interview.answer: The setting accepts `String | Array`. A single string identifies one view directory; an array provides multiple lookup directories.
interview.followUp: Why might an array be useful? It can combine application-specific templates with shared templates while preserving deterministic precedence.

interview.question: How does Express search multiple view directories?
interview.answer: Express resolves templates against the configured view directories. When an array is used, lookup follows array order, so directory ordering affects which template is selected.
interview.followUp: What related setting determines an extension when a rendered view omits one? `view engine` supplies the default template-engine extension.

keyPoints: The setting can point to one template directory or provide several directories.
Its documented type is `String | Array`, and the default path is based on the current working directory.
An array establishes the lookup precedence: Express checks entries from first to last.
Mounted sub-applications inherit this setting from the parent application.
gotchas: Mounted sub-applications inherit the configured `views` value, so set it explicitly when a sub-app needs a different template directory.
With multiple directories, an earlier directory wins when more than one contains a matching view.

x-powered-by.summary: `x-powered-by` is a Boolean Express application setting enabled by default. It controls whether responses include the `X-Powered-By: Express` header.
x-powered-by.explanation: Express stores this application setting as a Boolean that defaults to true. When enabled, responses include the X-Powered-By: Express header; use the application’s disable method with this setting name to turn it off.

example.title: Disable the Express power-by header
example.explanation: Creates an Express app and disables the identifying response header before serving requests.

useCases.title: Disable the identifying header
useCases.scenario: Reduce framework fingerprinting in production responses.

useCases.title: Configure parent and sub-app settings
useCases.scenario: Keep consistent application configuration across mounted Express applications.

useCases.title: Manage application settings
useCases.scenario: Inspect or change framework response behavior during setup.

interview.question: What does the `x-powered-by` setting control?
interview.answer: It is an Express application setting named `x-powered-by`. Its Boolean default is true, which enables the `X-Powered-By: Express` HTTP response header.
interview.followUp: How would you disable it? Call `app.disable('x-powered-by')` during application setup.

interview.question: How do you turn off the header?
interview.answer: Use `app.disable('x-powered-by')`. This disables the default header that identifies Express in responses.
interview.followUp: Does disabling it guarantee that Express cannot be identified? No; the documentation says sophisticated attackers may still determine that the app uses Express.

interview.question: What happens when an Express sub-app is mounted?
interview.answer: The setting is inherited by sub-applications. Therefore, a mounted sub-app inherits the parent application's value unless its configuration changes it.
interview.followUp: What type of setting is it? It is a Boolean application setting, and its default value is true.

keyPoints: The setting is named `x-powered-by`, accepts a Boolean, and is enabled by default.
When enabled, Express emits an `X-Powered-By: Express` response header.
Mounted Express sub-applications inherit the setting value from their parent application.
A newly configured Express application sends this response header unless the setting is changed.
gotchas: Turning the setting off is not a complete defense against identifying Express, because more sophisticated detection methods remain possible.
